title: Forces in Circular Motion
short: A real force such as tension, friction or gravity supplies the net inward force mv²/r.
trouble: Students add an outward "centrifugal force" to the free-body diagram, or think a released ball flies straight outward.

blocks.html: If an object has Centripetal Acceleration, the second law says a net force must point toward the center too. That force isn't a new kind of force. Some real push or pull, one you can name, does the job.

For motion in a circle, the net inward force is $\role[net inward force]{force}{\Sigma F_{in}} = \dfrac{\role{mass}{m}\role[speed]{velocity}{v}^2}{\role[radius]{position}{r}}$. Tension, friction, gravity or a normal force supplies it. Nothing pushes outward.

Without an inward force, an object moves in a straight line (the first law). The inward force keeps bending its path. On a flat road, the only horizontal force on a car is static friction from the road, so friction must supply all of $mv^2/r$; that sets a top speed, $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. For the Moon, Earth's gravity does the job; for a ball on a string, the tension does.

blocks.name: ph-circular

opts.task: Cut the string. Which way does the ball go?

blocks.cap: When the string is cut, the inward force disappears and the ball leaves along the tangent, not straight outward.

blocks.name: ph-circular
blocks.cap: On a flat curve, static friction points toward the center and supplies mv²/r.

blocks.title: Tension in a string
blocks.q: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ puck on frictionless ice circles a post at $4\ \text{m/s}$ on a $1.2\ \text{m}$ string. Find the tension.
steps: The string is the only horizontal force: $T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{(0.5)(16)}{1.2}$.

blocks.title: Top speed on a flat curve
blocks.q: How fast can a car take a flat curve of radius $40\ \text{m}$ if $\mu_s = 0.7$?
steps: At the limit, $\mu_s mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The mass cancels.

blocks.html: Adding an outward "centrifugal force" to the free-body diagram, or thinking a released ball flies straight outward. In a turning car you feel pushed outward because your body tends to keep going straight while the car turns under you. Check: every arrow on the diagram must be exerted by a real object, and a released object moves along the tangent.
